For the S. C. Herald.


CIRCULAR.


In view of the present pecuniary embarrassments in the country, the Executive Committee of the American Tract Society have been led seriously to inquire what course they ought to pursue. Shall their efforts be relaxed, and the bread of life withheld from perishing millions! The language of God is, 'Go forth; Christ has died, and an anxious world is pleading.'


SAVE THE WORLD.


In heathen countries, great facilities now exist for propagating the Gospel by the press: There are supported BY our foreign missionary societies, exclusively of Moravians, in heathen countries, six hundred and eighty three missionaries and assistants, four hundred and fourteen of whom have been sent out from the U. States, seventeen being printers; the remainder are native teachers, and printers.

Four hundred and forty-four Tracts and thirty-five volumes are issued in common with the American Tract Society, or approved by the publishing committee. The society and the various institutions aided, publish Tracts in fifty different languages embracing a very large part of the earth's population—the Nations asking for God's Law.


In a letter from Madras, dated, Oct. 25, 1836, Rev. Messrs. Winslow and Scudder say:


One of the great reasons why this missionary station has been commenced at Madras, is that the American Bible and Tract Societies may have the opportunity of distributing their productions to the millions to whom it opens the way of access. This, it appears, is the only hope legitimate for saving vast numbers that may soon be rescued from the wrath to come. To proclaim the Gospel (with the living voice) even to those speaking the Tamil language, a thousand men are needed. But where are they to be found? We would again earnest, that, to great extent, the only hope, humanly speaking, which can be entertained for the salvation of the present generation, IS it, what the American Bible & Tract Societies may do for them.


Our wants are the wants of as large a nation as that of the United States of America; six crore speaking the Tamil, and 90,000 speaking the Telugu language, to all of whom we may have access. The first grant we will beg of you is a sum sufficient to supply us with from 4,000 to 6,000 copies of The Blind Way, which is a very popular Tract. We have heard of one instance Gifts being torn up, the recipient stating that when he read it, he declared that this Tract was a great means of shaking his faith in superstitions. We think that 100,000 copies of this Blind Way, neatly bound in paper covers, could not cost less than 5,000 Spanish dollars. Perhaps you think 100,000 is a large edition. But when we consider that half this number might be distributed in Madras and its vicinity, and when we recollect that one of us distributed 5,000 Tracts in the course of six weeks, to small but distant portions of this country, we think that the demands of the people warrant us to go thus far.


From Ceylon, the claims are equally pressing. A letter from the Mission, dated Sept. 7, 1836, says: "The call for the Scriptures has increased the past year and will continue to increase every succeeding year. All that remain on hand might be easily and speedily disposed of in short time. There is no in the mission anything like a present supply of the word of life, or wants of it; nor is there likely to be supply for some time to come. How often have young men propounded to
themselves and others the question, what is the
first quality to be sought for the choice of wife
! and how diverse have been the answers to this
most important interrogatory! The gay and
thoughtless will point you to beauty, wealth, ac-
complishments: others, who look beyond the tin-
ction of the exterior, regard amiability and feeling
as the brightest jewels of the female character:
others still, who have searched deeper into the
springs of human action, and know well the
fountains whence flow the purest and most en-
during happiness, will give the only true answer
to the inquiry, viz: strong Christian senti-
ments and practice.


Religion is everywhere lovely, but in woman
peculiarly so; it makes her but little lower than
the angels. It purifies her heart, elevates her
feelings and sentiments, hallows her affections,
sheds light on her understanding, and imparts
dignity and pathos to her whole character. Nor
does its influence end here:


It beams in the glance of the eye,


It sits on the lip in a smile,


It checks the ungracious reply,


It enraptures, but cannot besiege.


Woman, from her very nature, is destined to
drink deeper from the cup of sorrow and suffer-
ing than the other sex. Her trials are chiefly of
the heart, and consequently the hardest to be
borne. She is seldom called upon to
contend with those formidable evils and tem-
tations which rouse all the energies of our nature
to repel their attack, but is beset (from the time
she merges into womanhood) by thousand per-
sonal trials and annoyances, which, while they seem
too insignificant, require much effort to resist,
are at the same time most difficult to overcome.
Religion alone can disarm these trials, and en-
able her to preserve that equanimity and peace of
mind so essential to happiness. It is her talisman. To it she flies in the hour of disappo'int-
ment and sorrow, and from it she derives
consolation and support. Yet how few, in their
selection of partner for life, regard this most
important qualification. How few think to pen-
etrate into the select chambers of the soul, to see
what is there hidden within, so far as an exterior; if
there the vestal lamp sheds its clear and constant
ray. External attractions may captivate us for
a time; feeling may send a thrill of exquisite
love through the heart of the recipient; talent
may call forth unbounded admiration; but if re-
ligion be not part of the character, the key-
stone to the arch is wanting, and the fabric will
crumble and fall.


It should be remembered that life is not all
shine. Bright as the world may be before us, we
cannot live long without encountering many sor-
rows, and disappointments, and troubles; they
are sent by a kind Providence to sever the cords
which bind us too closely to earth; to turn our
thoughts inward upon ourselves, and upward to
Heaven. While our bark glides calmly on sum-
mer's sea, with the blue sky above and bright
waters around us, these bland may soothe the
heart—but let it be overtaken by the storm
and the tempest, and where is the support then?
Let darkness enter your dwelling, and
the pleasure you derive from them is forgot;
Let death invade your social circle and lay his
ruthless hand on first-born, shroud all a-
round you in darkness and gloom, and where do
you look for a ray of hope! It is under cir-
cumstances like these that religion transforms her
into a ministering angel. She will bind up
your bleeding heart, lead you to the fountain of living
waters and change gloom and dependency into
light and cheerfulness. As the sun is setting,
it lights up every hilltop, and tree, and cottage, so
religion rides with its heavenly beams over every
feeling, enjoyment, and occupation.

loped in our nature, and the last touched by the

In one of the lOveliest villages of old Virginia there lived, in the year I775- an odd and old man, whose daughter was declared, by universal consent, to be the loveliest maiden inuall the country round. The veteran in his youth, had been athletic and muscular above all his fellows and his breast, where he always wore them, could show the adornment of three medals, received for his victories in gymnastic feats when young man. His daughter was now eighteen, and had been sought in mar riage by many suitors. One brought wealth-ano.ber a fine person-another this, and another that. But they were all refused by the old man, who became at last by-word for his obstinacy among the young men of the village and neighborhood. At length the nineteenth birth-day of Annette, his charming daughter, who was as aMiable and modest as she was beautiful, arrived. The merning of that day, her father invited all the youth of the country to a hay-making frolic. Seventeen hand- some and industrious young men assem- bled. They came not only to make hay, but also to make love to the fair Annette. In three hours they had filled ;he father's barns with the newly dried grass, and their own hearts with love. Annette, by her fathers command, had brought the malt li- quor of her own brewing, which she pre- sented to each enamoured swain with her own fair hands.

 Now my boys," said the old keeper of the jewel they all coveted, as. leaning on their pitch-forks, they assembled round his door in the cool of the evening"" Now my lads, you have nearly all of you made proposals for my Annette. Now you see, I don't care any thing about money or tal- ents, book larning nor soldier farming; ! can do as well by my gal as any man in the country. But want her to marry man ofmy own grit. Now, you know, or ought to know, when was youngster, I could beat any thing in all Virginny in the way O leaping. got my old woman by beat ing the smartest man on the Eastern Shore; and have took the oath, and swornit, that no man shall marry my daughter without jumping for it. You understand me, boys. There's the green, and here's Annette" he added, taking his daughter, who stood timidly behind him, by the hand. "Now, the one that jumps the furtherest on a dead level, shall marry Annette this'very night"

 This unique address was received by the young men with applause. And many a youth, as he bounded gaily forward to the arena of trial, cast a glance of anticipated victory back upon the lovely object of vil- lage chivally. The maidens left their looms and quilting frames-the children their noisy sports-,he slaves their labors, and the old men their arm-chairs and long pipes, to witness aud triumph in the suc- cess of the victor. All prophcsied, and many wished, that it would be young Car roll. He was the handsomest and best hu. mored youth in the country, and all knew that a strong and mutual attachment existed between him and the fair Annette. Car roll had won the repusation of being the best leaper;' and in country where such athletic achievements were the sine qua non' of mans cleverness, this was no or- dinary honor. In contest like the pres ent, he had therefore every advantage over his fellow 'athlete.'

 The arena allotted for this hymenial contest, was level space in front of the village inn, and near the centre of grass plat reserved in the midst of the village, denomina,ed the 'green.' The verdure was quite worn off at this place by the previous exercises of similar kind, and hard sur- face of sand be6uingly for the purpose to which it was to be used, supplied its place.

 The father of the lovely, blnshing, and withal HAPPY prize, (for she well knew who would win) with three other patriarch- al villagers, were the judges appointed to decide upon the claims of the several com- petitions. In one of the loveliest villages of old Virginia there lived, in the year 1775, an odd and old man, whose daughter was declared, by universal consent, to be the loveliest maiden in all the country round. The veteran in his youth, had been athletic and muscular above all his fellows and his breast, where he always wore them, could show the adornment of three medals, received for his victories in gymnastic feats when young man. His daughter was now eighteen, and had been sought in marriage by many suitors. One brought wealth—another a fine person—another this, and another that. But they were all refused by the old man, who became at last a by-word for his obstinacy among the young men of the village and neighborhood. At length the nineteenth birthday of Annette, his charming daughter, who was as amiable and modest as she was beautiful, arrived. The morning of that day, her father invited all the youth of the country to a hay-making frolic. Seventeen handsome and industrious young men assembled. They came not only to make hay, but also to make love to the fair Annette. In three hours they had filled the father's barns with the newly dried grass, and their own hearts with love. Annette, by her father's command, had brought the malt liquor of her own brewing, which she presented to each enamoured swain with her own fair hands.

"Now my boys," said the old keeper of the jewel they all coveted, as leaning on their pitch-forks, they assembled round his door in the cool of the evening. "Now my lads, you have nearly all of you made proposals for my Annette. Now you see, I don't care any thing about money or talents, book learning nor soldier farming; I can do as well by my gal as any man in the country. But want her to marry a man of my own grit. Now, you know, or ought to know, when I was a youngster, I could beat anything in all Virginny in the way of leaping; got my old woman by beating the smartest man on the Eastern Shore; and have took the oath, and sworn it, that no man shall marry my daughter without jumping for it. You understand me, boys. There's the green, and here's Annette," he added, taking his daughter, who stood timidly behind him, by the hand. "Now, the one that jumps the furthestest on a dead level, shall marry Annette this very night."

This unique address was received by the young men with applause. And many a youth, as he bounded gaily forward to the arena of trial, cast a glance of anticipated victory back upon the lovely object of village chivalry. The maidens left their looms and quilting frames—the children their noisy sports—the slaves their labors, and the old men their arm-chairs and long pipes, to witness a triumph in the success of the victor. All prophesied, and many wished, that it would be young Carroll.
